result:
There's a particular kind of silence that exists only in the gap between finishing one thought and starting another, and I think that's where most of the interesting material in a mind actually lives. Not in the thoughts themselves, which tend to be tidy and presentable, dressed up for an audience even when there's no audience around. The real texture is in the seams.

I want to write about nothing in particular, which is harder than it sounds, because the moment you give yourself permission to write about nothing, every subject rushes forward volunteering to be that nothing. The kettle in the kitchen. The way a word can lose its meaning if you stare at it too long—"the," for instance, becomes a strange little shape after the fortieth repetition, not a word at all but a hieroglyph, an artifact from a civilization that decided abstraction was worth the trouble. Language is a technology we've gotten so good at using that we forget it's a tool, the way you forget your glasses are on your face until someone asks you to clean them.

I keep coming back to attention as a subject, maybe because it's the only resource that actually feels finite in a day that otherwise stretches out in all directions with possibility. You can always make more money, theoretically. You can't make more attention, not in the same afternoon. It gets spent, and what it gets spent on becomes, in a very real sense, what your life was made of. People say "I don't have time" but what they usually mean is "I don't have attention to spare," because time, technically, they have plenty of—it's the bandwidth for noticing that runs short. A person can have eight free hours and still feel like they did nothing, because nothing held their focus long enough to leave a mark.

There's a theory, I think from somewhere in cognitive science, that boredom is actually attention searching for a worthy object and not finding one, like a dog padding from room to room. Boredom isn't emptiness; it's seeking with no target. Which would explain why scrolling a phone doesn't relieve boredom so much as it freezes the search mid-motion, offers the dog a tennis ball that turns out to be made of smoke. You bite down, there's nothing there, you go looking again.

I wonder sometimes if writing without a destination is its own form of that searching, except slower, and slowness might be the whole virtue of it. A sentence forces you to stay with one thought longer than a scroll does. You can't skip ahead in your own sentence; you have to build it, word by word, the way you'd lay bricks, and bricklaying, I imagine, gives you time to think about things unrelated to bricklaying, which is maybe why people who work with their hands often seem unusually settled, unusually present, even though their job is repetitive. Repetition frees the mind to wander precisely because the body doesn't need supervision.

I think about my grandmother peeling potatoes at the sink, not saying much, her hands doing the only complicated thing in the room while the rest of her seemed to be somewhere else entirely, maybe nowhere, maybe everywhere, the kind of peace that doesn't perform itself for company. I never asked her what she was thinking about. I assumed it was nothing, because nothing seemed to be the prevailing weather of that kitchen, but now I doubt that. Nothing is rarely actually nothing. It's usually just unlabeled.

There's a kind of writing that exists purely to fill space, and I worry, a little, that this is becoming that, but then I think—so what. Filling space honestly is its own kind of labor, no less real than filling it with a thesis or an argument. Not everything needs to arrive somewhere. Rivers don't apologize for meandering; the meander is the river doing exactly what rivers do, finding the lowest energy path through whatever ground it's given, which from above looks aimless and from the water's perspective is the only sensible route there is.

Maybe that's the closest thing to a thesis I have here: aimlessness, examined closely enough, turns out to have its own logic, its own quiet engineering. The thoughts that arrive without summons are sometimes more honest than the ones you go hunting for, because you can't pose for a thought you didn't choose to have. There's no vanity in noticing that the light through a window has gone the color of weak tea, or that a word like "threshold" sounds like what it means, has a little hinge built into its middle syllables. Those observations don't serve any argument. They just sit there, true and unbothered, asking nothing of you but to be seen for a second before the next one arrives.

I don't know how close to a thousand words this is, and that not-knowing feels appropriate, a small act of letting the form be a little out of my control, like leaving a door unlocked not because you expect anyone to come in but because locking it would mean deciding, ahead of time, exactly how the evening should go. Some sentences should be allowed to wander to the edge of the page and just stop, mid-thought almost, the way a walk ends not because you've arrived anywhere in particular but because your legs
